prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world the agent's observation shows the target shifted: the target, missing, extra and target-height channels are rolled 4 columns toward higher x, wrapping around. The world, its designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
The starting network scored 0 and learned to choose DONE straight away. The traces suggest why. The target as observed is the true design shifted cyclically along x by 4 columns (X/2). Every row of both diagnostic designs matches this, and rows are not shifted. Actions use the true positions: the untrained agent's first placement was on an observed target cell, yet it got -0.093, which means that cell is outside the true target. The starting network sees only 2–3 cells around each position and uses zero padding, so it cannot connect an action at x to the observation at x+4. With nothing to learn from, every placement looks bad and DONE (reward 0) wins. The main bet is to give the network learned layers that can move information anywhere along each axis or across the grid. These layers must stay general: no hard-coded shift, and any grid size. This round also tests whether more exploration and more samples per unit of compute help keep the agent from settling on DONE.

### Round 2
Both diagnostic traces show that the observed target is the true design shifted cyclically by 4 columns (X/2) in x, with rows unchanged. Networks that only see a local neighbourhood cannot line up the target with the action positions. They find nothing useful to learn and collapse to DONE at step 1: the start, the transformer and r1c3 all did this. r1c1 (AxisMix) learned to undo the shift on seed 0: its greedy placements land at the true design positions, mean IoU is 0.63 and success is 0.6%. Its seed 1 still collapsed, so it escapes collapse only some of the time. It also stops too early. Training is only about 27 updates. Plan: (A) a cheap, general learned full-row and full-column circular convolution front end, so alignment is easy to learn early, before collapse; (B) r1c1 with about twice as many updates for the same samples; (C) A plus B's recipe.

### Round 3
The observed target is shifted cyclically in x by X/2: design column c appears at column c+4 mod 8. To use it, a cell must see its whole row. Circular full-row and full-column convolutions (r2c1, r2c3) solved this at 0.32 and 0.35. Per-channel axis-mix (r1c1, r2c2) scored only 0.00 to 0.04, and attention (r1c2) collapsed to DONE. Running more updates with n_envs 128 helped both front ends, but r2c3's seeds differ a lot (0.62 vs 0.08), so that gain is uncertain. Training success in r2c3 was still rising at the end (0.24, then 0.37, then 0.54), so the run looks budget-limited. The likely next gains are more samples or updates and better global reasoning about build order and when to stop. Each refinement makes one recipe change to r2c3. The new idea adds circular row and column mixing to the deeper features.

### Round 4
The traces show that the target channels are shifted cyclically in x by X/2. Front ends that see a whole row and column through circular convolutions handle this shift on both seeds; per-channel mixing matrices (r1c1, r2c2) and attention (r1c2) handled it poorly or not at all. Adding row/column mixing deeper in the network (r3c3, 0.46) beat the front-end-only version (r2c3, 0.35), and its two seeds were closer together. That gap is still near the noise level. Recipe changes are risky: both 2 PPO epochs and 64 envs made both seeds collapse to DONE first, even with a good network. So the r3c3 recipe stays fixed for the architecture changes. Training success was still rising at the end of r3c3, but the budget trades samples against compute. Since this is the last round, the candidates are: one more global row/column block, wider row/column channels, and one careful change to the discount aimed at the end-of-episode bonus for an exact build.

## Trial it ended with
name: r3c3 with wider row/col channels
hypothesis: Widen the circular row/column convolutions from 24 to 40 channels in the front end and from 20 to 28 in the deep block. Undoing the X/2 shift for every target, missing and height channel needs roughly one output channel per shifted input channel, so 24 ReLU channels may be a bottleneck for exact per-layer alignment. Compute rises to about 1.8x. Refuted if the mean is at or below 0.46.

Return a JSON object: "verdict" ("yes", "partly" or "no") and "evidence" (at most 80 words, quoting the text and
naming the round it comes from).

reply.evidence: Round 1 says: "The target as observed is the true design shifted cyclically along x by 4 columns (X/2)... rows are not shifted." Round 3 gives the direction: "design column c appears at column c+4 mod 8", which is a wrap-around shift toward higher x. The final trial adds that the shift covers the "target, missing and height" channels. Together these state the rule: the observed target channels are rolled 4 columns toward higher x, with wrap-around.
